body.en: A single integral \( \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \) sums up \( f \) over an interval; a double integral \( \iint_R f(x,y)\,dA \) sums \( f \) over a whole region \( R \) of the plane, and (for \( f\ge0 \)) gives the volume under the surface \( z=f(x,y) \). The one new practical question is how to actually compute one — and the answer is to reduce it to two ordinary, single-variable integrals, done one after the other.

label.en: ● Definition 4.1 — Double integral over a rectangle

body.en: For \( f \) continuous on \( R=[a,b]\times[c,d] \), partition \( R \) into an \( m\times n \) grid of sub-rectangles \( R_{ij} \), each of area \( \Delta A=\Delta x\,\Delta y \), and pick a sample point \( (x_i^*,y_j^*)\in R_{ij} \). The double integral is the limit of the Riemann sum as the grid is refined: \[ \iint_R f\,dA=\lim_{m,n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta A. \]

An iterated integral computes one variable at a time: \[ \int_a^b\!\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx \] means: first integrate \( f(x,y) \) with respect to \( y \) (treating \( x \) as a constant) from \( c \) to \( d \), producing a function of \( x \) alone, then integrate that result with respect to \( x \) from \( a \) to \( b \).

The double integral (Definition 4.1) and the iterated integral (Definition 4.2) are computed completely differently — one is a genuine two-dimensional limit, the other is two ordinary one-dimensional integrals in sequence. The theorem that makes double integrals practical to compute is that, for continuous \( f \), they always agree.

If \( f \) is continuous on \( R=[a,b]\times[c,d] \), then \[ \iint_R f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx=\int_c^d\!\!\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy. \] This holds for every continuous \( f \) on a rectangle — the fully general proof (which needs the uniform continuity of \( f \) on the compact rectangle \( R \)) belongs to a real analysis course. Below we prove it in full for the case that actually drives how you'll split integrals apart in practice: a separable integrand \( f(x,y)=g(x)h(y) \).

Fix any partition of \( R \) into sub-rectangles \( R_{ij} \) with sample points \( (x_i^*,y_j^*) \), as in Definition 4.1. Because \( f(x_i^*,y_j^*)=g(x_i^*)h(y_j^*) \), the double Riemann sum factors exactly — for every partition, not just in a limit — by distributivity: \[ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}f(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}g(x_i^*)h(y_j^*)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{m}g(x_i^*)\Delta x\Big)\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n}h(y_j^*)\Delta y\Big). \]

As the grid is refined (\( m,n\to\infty \)), the two factors on the right are ordinary single-variable Riemann sums, converging (since \( g,h \) are continuous, hence Riemann integrable) to \( \int_a^b g(x)\,dx \) and \( \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \) respectively. Since both factors converge, their product converges to the product of the limits: \[ \iint_R f\,dA=\Big(\int_a^b g(x)\,dx\Big)\Big(\int_c^d h(y)\,dy\Big). \]

This is exactly the value of either iterated integral: \( \int_a^b\!\int_c^d g(x)h(y)\,dy\,dx=\int_a^b g(x)\Big[\int_c^d h(y)\,dy\Big]dx=\Big(\int_c^d h(y)\,dy\Big)\int_a^b g(x)\,dx \), since \( \int_c^d h(y)\,dy \) is a constant with respect to \( x \) and pulls out of the outer integral — and symmetrically for the other order. All three quantities are equal.

label.en: Worked example 4.A — Order of integration doesn't matter

body.en:
Compute \( \iint_R(x^2+y)\,dA \) for \( R=[0,2]\times[0,1] \), both orders.

\[ \int_0^2\!\!\int_0^1(x^2+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^2\Big[x^2y+\tfrac{y^2}{2}\Big]_0^1dx=\int_0^2\Big(x^2+\tfrac12\Big)dx=\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}+\tfrac{x}{2}\Big]_0^2=\tfrac83+1=\tfrac{11}{3}. \]

\[ \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2(x^2+y)\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1\Big[\tfrac{x^3}{3}+xy\Big]_0^2dy=\int_0^1\Big(\tfrac83+2y\Big)dy=\Big[\tfrac83y+y^2\Big]_0^1=\tfrac83+1=\tfrac{11}{3}. \]

Same value either way, as Theorem 4.1 guarantees — \( x^2+y \) isn't separable, but it's still continuous on \( R \), so the general (unproved-here) case of Fubini applies.

When a region is naturally circular, switch to polar coordinates \( x=r\cos\theta \), \( y=r\sin\theta \). A small polar "rectangle" spanning \( [r,r+\Delta r]\times[\theta,\theta+\Delta\theta] \) has one pair of sides of length \( \Delta r \) (radial) and the other pair of approximate length \( r\,\Delta\theta \) (arc length at radius \( r \)), so its area is approximately \( r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta \) rather than \( \Delta r\,\Delta\theta \) — the extra factor of \( r \) is exactly why \( dA=r\,dr\,d\theta \), not \( dr\,d\theta \), and why \( x^2+y^2 \) becomes the clean \( r^2 \).

label.en: Worked example 4.B — A double integral in polar coordinates

body.en:
Compute \( \iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA \) where \( D \) is the disk \( x^2+y^2\le4 \).

In polar coordinates, \( D \) is \( 0\le r\le2 \), \( 0\le\theta\le2\pi \), and \( x^2+y^2=r^2 \), \( dA=r\,dr\,d\theta \): \[ \iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2 r^2\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\Big[\frac{r^4}{4}\Big]_0^2 d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}4\,d\theta=8\pi. \]

The integrand is separable in polar form (\( r^3 \) times \( 1 \)), which is exactly why the \( r \)- and \( \theta \)-integrals split apart so cleanly — the same factoring idea proved in Theorem 4.1.
